Fashion designs are partially protected under copyright law, but the scope of protection varies by country and depends on whether the design contains sufficient creativity or utilitarian functionality. [d1] In the United States, the Copyright Office has stated that two-dimensional designs on clothing surfaces, fabric designs, and logos can qualify for copyright protection if they demonstrate a minimal amount of creativity, while clothing itself is not protected to the same extent as other creative works [d1][d2][d3]. However, designs that are purely functional or utilitarian in nature — such as clothing's color, texture, or basic shape — are generally not protected under copyright law, which favors utility over aesthetics [d4][d2]. In the European Union, fashion designs can receive protection for up to three or five years under the Creative Designs Directive, though this protection applies only to new designs and does not cover all fashion designs broadly [d2][d3].

A landmark court case involving the poem helped protect First Amendment rights and paved the way for freedom of speech in art, though the poem remains the subject of ongoing censorship debates today [d4][d5]. Historians and legal scholars note that the 1957 ruling was a significant victory for First Amendment protections, as Judge Horn explicitly stated that 'no two persons think alike; we were all made from the same mold but in different patterns' and that reducing vocabulary to innocuous euphemisms would undermine freedom of press and speech [d5], a ruling that has been celebrated as a classic defense of artistic expression [d2].
[[END-OF-ANSWER]]
